title: The Battle of Badr
subtitle: The Day of Criterion, Divine Aid, and the Fall of Tyranny
summary: The convergence at the wells of Badr on the seventeenth of Ramadan, the strategic counsel of Al-Hubab ibn al-Mundhir, the Prophet's fervent supplication in the command shelter, the heroic opening duels, divine support through angels, and the decisive victory establishing the reality of the Islamic state.

sections.text: Convergence at the Wells of Badr

On the evening of Thursday, the sixteenth of Ramadan in the second year after the Hijrah (March 624 CE), the Muslim contingent arrived at the desert valley of Badr, approximately eighty miles southwest of Madinah. Badr was a famous staging station on the caravan route, distinguished by several subterranean water wells surrounded by steep sand dunes. The Muslims encamped at the first well they reached on the eastern edge of the valley.

The exchange that follows is classical sirah, not a wording cited here from a numbered hadith. An experienced warrior of the Ansar, Al-Hubab ibn al-Mundhir, approached the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ with great respect and inquired: 'O Messenger of God, is this camp a position chosen through divine revelation which we may neither advance beyond nor retreat from, or is it a matter of military opinion, strategy, and warfare?' The Prophet replied with characteristic openness: 'Rather, it is a matter of military opinion, strategy, and warfare.'

Al-Hubab advised: 'O Messenger of God, this is not the right camp. Lead the men forward until we reach the well nearest to the enemy. We shall encamp there, fill up and seal all the other wells behind us, and construct a large reservoir of water. Thus, when we fight the enemy, we will have water to drink while they will have none.' The Prophet embraced the practical advice with immediate humility, ordering the army to advance and execute the tactical plan.
The arid desert dunes of Badr where the historic confrontation took place.
The Night of Rain and the Arish

The sirah says that Sa'd ibn Mu'adh proposed constructing a shaded command post (Al-Arish) atop an elevated hillock overlooking the battlefield. He placed swift riding camels nearby, assuring the Prophet: 'Stay in your shelter, O Messenger of God; if God grants us victory, that is what we desire; and if the worst happens, you may ride swiftly back to our people in Madinah, for behind you are folk who love you no less than we do, who would defend you with their lives.'

That night, God sent down a gentle, refreshing rain upon the valley. For the Muslims, the rain compacted the loose desert sand underfoot, purified them, and allowed them to sink into deep, tranquil sleep. For Quraysh on the opposite clay ridge, the deluge transformed the earth into sticky, treacherous mud. The Quran commemorates this divine blessing in Surah Al-Anfal: 'When He caused you to be overcome with slumber as a security from Him and sent down upon you rain from the heaven to purify you...' (8:11).

At dawn the two lines met. Muslim 1763 numbers the Prophet's companions that day at three hundred and nineteen, and the other side at one thousand. Other reports say three hundred and thirteen. The shelter of branches is the sirah. The supplication, with the cloak falling from his shoulders and Abu Bakr putting it back, is the opening of that same hadith of Umar, which later in the report also contains the consultation about the captives:

اللَّهُمَّ أَنْجِزْ لِي مَا وَعَدْتَنِي، اللَّهُمَّ آتِ مَا وَعَدْتَنِي، اللَّهُمَّ إِنْ تَهْلِكْ هَذِهِ الْعِصَابَةُ مِنْ أَهْلِ الْإِسْلَامِ لَا تُعْبَدْ فِي الْأَرْضِ
'O God, fulfill for me what You have promised me. O God, bring what You have promised me. O God, if this band of the people of Islam is destroyed, You will not be worshipped on the earth.' (Sahih Muslim 1763)

Moved by his tears, Abu Bakr stepped forward, replaced the cloak upon the Prophet's shoulders, and embraced him gently, saying: 'O Messenger of God, enough of your petitioning your Lord, for indeed He will surely fulfill what He has promised you!'
The mountain slopes of the Hijaz where faith conquered overwhelming numbers.
The Opening Duels and the Clash

The sirah opens the fighting with single combat. The speeches are that account, not a dialogue invented for this chapter. Three champion warriors of Quraysh stepped into the neutral zone between the armies: the brothers Utbah and Shaybah, sons of Rabi'ah, alongside Utbah's son, al-Walid. Three youths of the Ansar stepped forward to meet them, but the Makkan chiefs shouted: 'O Muhammad! Send forth our equals from our own noble clan!'

The Prophet called out: 'Rise, O Ubaydah ibn al-Harith! Rise, O Hamzah! Rise, O Ali!' In swift, electrifying clashes, Hamzah struck down Shaybah, young Ali swiftly dispatched al-Walid, and together they assisted Ubaydah after he was mortally wounded by Utbah, carrying him back to the Muslim lines. The loss of three paramount leaders in the opening minutes shattered the morale of Quraysh.
The Decisive Rout and Divine Aid

Quraysh launched a massive general assault. The Prophet emerged from the shelter clad in armor, grasped a handful of desert gravel, and cast it toward the enemy lines, exclaiming: 'May their faces be distorted!' (Shahat al-wujuh). The Quran confirms: 'And you threw not, [O Muhammad], when you threw, but it was God who threw' (8:17). A miraculous sand-laden gale blew directly into the eyes of the Makkan warriors, and angels descended in ranks to steady the hearts of the believers.

Muslim 1763 says that on that day they killed seventy and captured seventy. The sirah's count of Muslims killed is fourteen. The killing of Abu Jahl, as the maghazi narrations tell it, was at the hands of the two sons of Afra, Mu'adh and Mu'awwidh, and Abdullah ibn Mas'ud finished him. The Quran calls the day the Day of the Criterion. The field did not make the community safe from every later battle.
